strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical problem: producing pixel-dense features from pretrained visual backbones without paying the quadratic cost of dense ViT inference or cross-attention upsamplers.

The proposed UPLiFT architecture is technically plausible and well motivated. The Local Attender gives a simple local linear-combination mechanism that preserves feature-distribution constraints while scaling linearly in the number of tokens.

Empirical results on dense prediction are solid. On DINOv2-S/14, UPLiFT improves over strong recent feature upsampling baselines on COCO-Stuff, VOC, ADE20K, and Cityscapes segmentation, while being faster than LoftUp, JAFAR, AnyUp, and FeatUp in the reported pixel-dense setting.

The paper includes useful ablations: training depth, Local Attender neighborhood size, removal of Local Attender, DINOv3 results, memory/time scaling, and qualitative PCA visualizations of feature stability. These help support the main architectural claims.

The extension to VAE latent upsampling is interesting and potentially useful. The results suggest that the same general idea can provide efficient latent upsampling for generation and super-resolution, which broadens the contribution beyond dense prediction.
weaknesses: The main performance gains in dense prediction are consistent but modest for several datasets, e.g. COCO and ADE20K improvements over AnyUp/JAFAR/LoftUp are relatively small, so the acceptance case relies heavily on efficiency and scaling rather than a large accuracy jump.

The generative-task evaluation is less convincing than the dense-prediction evaluation. Several CFM numbers are adapted from prior work, reLAION is not exactly the same dataset due to deprecation, and some comparisons mix methods with different training data, model sizes, sampling steps, and task specialization. This makes the state-of-the-art generative claims somewhat overstated.

For super-resolution, UPLiFT has better SSIM/PSNR on some metrics but substantially worse FID and patch-FID than CFM on FacesHQ and LHQ. The paper frames this as competitive, but the perceptual-quality gap is material and should temper the claims.

The Local Attender is elegant, but its originality is incremental relative to existing local/windowed attention, dynamic filtering, and local aggregation ideas. The paper would benefit from a sharper positioning of what is fundamentally new beyond a learned local softmax kernel applied during iterative upsampling.

The evaluation is mostly based on linear probes over frozen features. This is appropriate for feature quality, but it leaves open how much the gains transfer to stronger dense-task pipelines or end-to-end adaptation settings.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code and models are only promised for release at publication. Some implementation details are in the appendix, but exact training recipes, optimizer settings, and baseline reproduction details appear insufficient for full independent verification.

The VAE version introduces extra components such as a Refiner Block, noise channels, LayerNorm changes, and post-hoc color correction. These practical additions are reasonable, but they make the generative contribution less cleanly attributable to the proposed Local Attender mechanism.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: producing dense visual features from pretrained backbones with lower inference cost than direct high-resolution backbone inference or global cross-attention upsamplers.

The proposed UPLiFT design is simple and practical. Iterative 2x upsampling with a dense image encoder and the Local Attender operator gives a clear efficiency rationale, and the claimed O(nT) local pooling cost is technically plausible when the neighborhood size is fixed.

The predictive-task evaluation is reasonably broad for this niche: semantic segmentation on COCO-Stuff, VOC, ADE20K, and Cityscapes, plus monocular depth on COCO, with comparisons to LiFT, FeatUp, LoftUp, JAFAR, AnyUp, and interpolation baselines.

The reported results are consistent: UPLiFT slightly improves segmentation mIoU/accuracy across all four datasets and is competitive on depth, while being faster than the recent cross-attention upsamplers at the tested resolution.

The paper includes useful ablations for training depth and Local Attender neighborhood size. The large drop without Local Attender supports the claim that this component is important for stable iterative upsampling.

The efficiency/scaling plots and memory measurements are a meaningful contribution, especially because practical dense-feature methods can be limited more by memory and latency than by small benchmark differences.
weaknesses: The core novelty is limited. Local Attender is essentially a learned local dynamic filtering/content-aware reassembly mechanism with fixed offsets and softmax weights, closely related in spirit to prior local upsampling, CARAFE-like operators, dynamic filters, and local/windowed attention. The paper does not sufficiently position or empirically compare against matched local/dynamic convolutional alternatives, so the claimed conceptual contribution feels overstated.

The main predictive-task accuracy gains are small. For example, segmentation improvements over AnyUp/JAFAR/LoftUp are often fractions of a point, and depth is not clearly better than AnyUp. The strongest case is efficiency, but the paper frames the method as state of the art in performance more strongly than the evidence warrants.

The fairness of comparisons is not fully convincing. Some baseline numbers are recomputed after modifying the JAFAR evaluation schedule, some are adapted from prior work, and the paper does not provide enough detail to judge whether all methods received equally optimized training, resizing, compilation, batching, and hardware treatment.

The universality claim is under-supported. Most main results use DINOv2-S/14, with limited supplemental DINOv3 segmentation results. There is little evidence across backbone families such as CLIP, SigLIP, MAE, MoCo, or larger DINO variants, despite the method name and framing as universal.

The generative-task section is considerably weaker than the predictive section. Comparisons to CFM rely partly on adapted numbers, reLAION is described as only 'sufficiently similar' to LAION, diffusion-step settings for CFM are uncertain, and the evaluation lacks human preference, perceptual quality metrics, or robust artifact analysis. FID/patch-FID alone is a thin basis for strong claims about image generation and super-resolution quality.

The VAE upsampling method introduces extra components such as a large 53M-parameter model, noise channels, a refiner block, layer norm changes, and post-hoc color correction. These additions weaken the clean story that Local Attender alone preserves feature distributions, and their interactions are not quantitatively ablated enough.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper says code and models will be released at publication, but the manuscript itself lacks many implementation details needed to reproduce the results confidently, including full architecture specifications, optimizer schedules, training compute, exact preprocessing, and baseline timing methodology.

Several claims are too broad or imprecise. Statements such as achieving state-of-the-art performance across predictive and generative domains, maintaining feature semantics, and matching CFM visual fidelity are stronger than the evidence presented. The paper would be more convincing with narrower claims centered on efficient dense feature upsampling.

The analysis of semantic drift is mostly visual PCA evidence. This is suggestive, but there is no quantitative measure of feature distribution preservation, local semantic consistency, or drift accumulation across iterative steps.

Overall, the work has practical merit and some solid evidence, especially on efficiency, but the originality and evaluation rigor are not strong enough for a confident acceptance recommendation at CVPR.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practical problem: producing dense features from pretrained visual backbones without paying the full cost of high-resolution ViT inference. The motivation is clear and the efficiency angle is important for dense prediction workloads.

The proposed UPLiFT design is technically plausible and well explained. The Local Attender gives a simple local linear-combination mechanism that preserves feature-distribution consistency while avoiding global cross-attention, yielding linear scaling in the number of visual tokens.

The experimental evidence for predictive tasks is strong. On DINOv2-S/14, UPLiFT improves over FeatUp, LoftUp, JAFAR, AnyUp, LiFT, bilinear, and nearest-neighbor baselines across four segmentation datasets, while also being faster than the recent high-performing upsamplers. The DINOv3 appendix adds useful evidence that the approach transfers beyond a single backbone family variant.

The paper includes meaningful ablations. The removal of Local Attender causes a large drop in segmentation performance, and the neighborhood-size and training-depth studies support the main architectural and training choices.

The efficiency analysis is a notable strength. The paper reports timing and memory scaling on A5000/A6000 GPUs and shows that cross-attention-based methods run out of memory earlier, while UPLiFT continues to larger token counts with better speed.

The extension to VAE latent upsampling is interesting and broadens the paper beyond standard dense prediction. The results suggest UPLiFT can be useful as a general latent-feature upsampler for super-resolution and diffusion-output upscaling.
weaknesses: The novelty is solid but somewhat incremental. The method combines iterative upsampling, image-guided convolutional decoding, and local content-dependent pooling; the Local Attender is effective, but it is conceptually close to dynamic local filtering/content-aware reassembly style operators. The paper could better distinguish the operator from prior local feature reassembly and dynamic filtering methods beyond contrasting it with cross-attention.

Some headline claims are broader than the evidence. The term “Universal” is not fully supported: the predictive model is trained for specific backbone features, AnyUp is discussed as more backbone-general, and the generative experiments require a much larger separately trained UPLiFT with extra components such as a refiner block, noise inputs, layer norm changes, and color correction.

The generative-task comparisons are promising but less controlled than the predictive-task comparisons. Several CFM rows are adapted from prior work, dataset details differ in places such as reLAION versus deprecated LAION, and CFM models may be dataset-specific while UPLiFT is presented as general-purpose. These differences make the efficiency and quality claims credible but not as cleanly isolated as the dense-prediction evaluation.

The generative results show mixed tradeoffs. UPLiFT improves SSIM/PSNR in some super-resolution settings, but CFM has much better FID and patch-FID on FacesHQ and LHQ. The text emphasizes competitiveness and efficiency, which is fair, but the visual-fidelity claim should be moderated given the perceptual metric gap.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time. The paper says code and models will be released at publication, but the manuscript currently relies on many implementation details, recomputed baselines, timing protocols, and modified evaluation settings that would be hard to independently verify without the release.

The evaluation would be stronger with additional downstream tasks and more backbone diversity in the main paper. Segmentation and one depth setup are useful, but dense correspondence, object boundaries, detection/instance segmentation, or more foundation backbones would better support the general feature-upsampling claims.

There are a few presentation and correctness nits: Table 7 appears to repeat 84.80 for both VOC mIoU and accuracy in the n=5 row, and some generative claims around “single step” versus “two iterative upsampling steps” could be stated more consistently. These do not undermine the main contribution but should be cleaned up.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and useful problem: efficient task-agnostic upsampling of dense visual features. The proposed UPLiFT design is practically motivated and targets a real limitation of recent cross-attention upsamplers, namely poor scaling with token count.

The Local Attender operator is simple, technically plausible, and well matched to the goal: it constrains upsampled features to local linear combinations of backbone features while using high-resolution guide features for spatial detail. Its linear-in-token complexity is clearly argued.

The predictive-task evaluation is relatively broad for this area. The paper reports semantic segmentation across COCO-Stuff, VOC, ADE20K, and Cityscapes, plus depth estimation, and compares against relevant recent feature upsamplers including FeatUp, LiFT, LoftUp, JAFAR, and AnyUp variants.

Empirical results support the main efficiency-quality claim. UPLiFT obtains consistent segmentation improvements over prior upsamplers while being substantially faster than the strongest cross-attention baselines at 448x448, and the scaling plots show a meaningful advantage at larger token counts.

The ablations are useful and targeted: training depth, Local Attender neighborhood size, removal of Local Attender, encoder/decoder capacity, and replacement with windowed cross-attention all help justify the architectural choices.
The paper also explores VAE latent upsampling for generative tasks, which is an interesting extension beyond the usual dense prediction setting and suggests broader usefulness of the approach.
weaknesses: The performance gains on predictive tasks, while consistent, are fairly modest on several datasets and metrics. For example, segmentation improvements over AnyUp/JAFAR/LoftUp are often within about 0.3-1.0 mIoU except Cityscapes, and no variance across random seeds or statistical uncertainty is reported.

The originality of Local Attender is somewhat incremental relative to prior local dynamic filtering, content-aware reassembly, neighborhood attention, and feature upsampling operators. The paper compares to windowed cross-attention but does not deeply position the operator against older content-aware local aggregation methods such as CARAFE/SAPA-style upsamplers beyond general related work.

The generative-task evidence is less convincing than the predictive-task evidence. UPLiFT is faster and smaller than CFM, but in super-resolution its FID and patch-FID are much worse than CFM on both FacesHQ and LHQ, despite better SSIM/PSNR in some cases. The claim of competitive generative quality therefore depends heavily on which metrics are emphasized.

Some generative comparisons are not fully controlled. Several CFM rows are adapted from prior work, the reLAION evaluation replaces the original LAION setup, diffusion-step settings for CFM are partly unclear, and there is no user study or stronger perceptual metric such as LPIPS/DISTS to support visual-quality claims.

The efficiency reporting would be more useful if it more explicitly separated and also combined backbone/generator cost, upsampler cost, preprocessing/decoding cost, and optimized-kernel assumptions. UPLIFTFAST relies on engineering optimizations such as a fused Triton kernel and torch.compile, which are valuable but may complicate fair comparison if baselines are not similarly optimized.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time. The manuscript says code and models will be released at publication, but the review must evaluate the current manuscript; exact implementation details are partly deferred to a future repository, especially for module configurations and optimized kernels.

The evaluation mainly uses linear probes over upsampled features at a fixed resolution for predictive tasks. This is appropriate for the feature-upsampling literature, but it leaves open how much the method improves stronger task-specific heads, full fine-tuning pipelines, detection/instance segmentation, or downstream systems where end-to-end cost and accuracy matter.

There are minor presentation and consistency issues, such as apparent table/text typos in the appendix and some overstrong phrasing around state-of-the-art generative performance given mixed metric results. These do not undermine the central contribution but should be tightened.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant efficiency problem in dense feature extraction: producing pixel-dense features from pretrained backbones without paying the full cost of high-resolution ViT inference.
weaknesses: The main technical idea, Local Attender, appears closer to a lightweight content-adaptive local filtering/resampling operator than a fundamentally new attention mechanism. The paper does not sufficiently position it against older dynamic filtering/content-aware upsampling families such as CARAFE/JBU-like methods, so the originality claim feels overstated.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and useful problem: producing pixel-dense features from strong pretrained backbones at substantially lower cost than rerunning dense ViTs or using global cross-attention upsamplers.

The proposed UPLiFT design is technically plausible and well motivated. The Local Attender is a simple local, guide-conditioned pooling operator with linear scaling in token count, and the paper clearly connects it to the semantic drift problem observed in iterative feature upsampling.

The predictive-task evidence is strong overall. On DINOv2-S/14, UPLiFT improves over prior task-agnostic feature upsamplers on semantic segmentation across COCO, VOC, ADE20K, and Cityscapes, while being faster than the stronger learned baselines. The depth results are also competitive, tying the best RMSE and falling only slightly behind AnyUp on delta-1.

The efficiency case is convincing: the paper reports latency, scaling behavior, memory scaling in the appendix, and an optimized fast mode. The comparison against cross-attention methods and AnyUp-v2/NATTEN makes the practical advantage easy to understand.

The ablation section is useful. The manuscript studies training depth, Local Attender neighborhood design, encoder/decoder size, removal of the encoder, comparison to windowed cross-attention, non-ViT backbones, and DINOv3 segmentation. These experiments support the main design choices rather than only reporting headline numbers.

The extension to VAE latent upsampling is a valuable addition. Even though not uniformly better than specialized generative baselines, it broadens the contribution and shows that the same general idea can be useful beyond discriminative dense prediction.
weaknesses: The originality of the Local Attender is somewhat incremental relative to dynamic local filtering, local attention, and neighborhood attention. The paper distinguishes it from QKV/NATTEN, but the conceptual advance is more an efficient and well-engineered formulation for this application than a fundamentally new attention mechanism.

Several predictive-task gains are modest in absolute terms. For example, segmentation improvements over LoftUp/JAFAR/AnyUp are often under one mIoU point, so the acceptance case relies heavily on the combined performance-efficiency tradeoff rather than a large accuracy advance.

The predictive evaluation is still mostly linear-probe based at 448x448. This is appropriate for comparing task-agnostic features, but it leaves open how much the gains transfer to stronger downstream decoders, end-to-end fine-tuning, higher-resolution dense prediction, detection/instance segmentation, or more varied real deployment settings.

The generative-task evidence is more mixed than the prose sometimes suggests. For super-resolution, UPLiFT improves SSIM/PSNR but is much worse than CFM on FID and patch-FID, especially on FacesHQ. This indicates weaker perceptual realism despite good distortion metrics, and should temper the claim of state-of-the-art generative quality.

Some generative comparisons are not perfectly controlled. Several CFM rows are adapted from prior work, the reLAION setup differs from the deprecated LAION setting used by CFM, and the paper notes uncertainty about diffusion steps for CFM. These choices are reasonable but reduce confidence in fine-grained claims about superiority.

The VAE version introduces additional components such as a larger model, noise inputs, a refiner block, layer normalization changes, and post-decoder color correction. These are practical, but they make the generative setting less clean as evidence for the same core Local Attender contribution.

Reproducibility is decent in terms of described protocols and pseudocode, but the paper states that code and models will be released at publication rather than being available for review. Exact implementation details for the optimized fast mode, Triton kernel, training configs, and possible variance over runs are therefore hard to independently verify from the manuscript alone.
